title: Temperature, Humidity, Pressure
about: How heat energy, water vapour and air weight shape weather and life.
principles: Heat transfer, evaporation/condensation, gas laws, air pressure gradients.
philosophy: Change is constant; invisible forces knit life together; balance keeps ecosystems alive.
experiments: Build a simple barometer (jar + balloon) and homemade hygrometer (hair strand or salt-in-jar).
home: Map temperatures in different rooms at different times; compare fridge, sunny window.
outdoors: Dawn walk to feel temperature drop and morning dew; compare hilltop vs valley air pressure using ears/pop.
dance: Group creates “rising heat” moves—slow stretch to fast spiral.
drama: Short play: Invisible air arguing with visible water about who controls weather.
art: Draw a “map of invisible forces”: heat waves, humidity clouds, pressure arrows.
music: Compose soundscape of dripping taps, kettle hiss, whistling wind.
yoga: Practice alternate-nostril breathing noticing cool inhale / warm exhale.
physical_games: “Pressure tag”: tagged child must crouch (low pressure) until another “high pressure” rescues.
games: Card game: match weather symbols to their effect on people/plants.
reading: “Clouds in a Glass” (Franklyn Branley) or kid-level meteorology books.
writing: Journal a day’s weather as a letter from the sky to the Earth.
more: Build a mini greenhouse with plastic wrap to watch humidity cycle.
other: Photograph morning condensation on leaves; compare over days.

title: Winds & Circulation (Coriolis, trade winds, jet streams)
about: Global and local air movements driven by Earth’s rotation and heating.
principles: Coriolis effect, pressure belts, Hadley cells, jet stream dynamics.
philosophy: Movement and rotation create order; invisible motion connects continents.
experiments: Spin a turntable with a chalk mark to show Coriolis spiral; create mini “Hadley cell” with warm lamp and ice bowl.
home: Use a handheld fan and incense stick to visualise local breezes.
outdoors: Fly kites in open field; observe wind direction with homemade ribbon wind-vanes.
dance: “Spiral dance”: arms wide, turning like Earth, tracing air currents.
drama: Skit: “East Wind meets West Wind” debating who brings the rains.
art: Paint world map with swirling arrows of global wind belts.
music: Make a wind-chime orchestra; let random gusts play the tune.
yoga: Long, slow “wind breath”: inhale with arms up, exhale while twisting like a cyclone.
physical_games: Parachute game: kids create waves of “wind belts” with a large sheet.
games: Board-game design: players move tokens using “trade wind cards”.
reading: Read excerpts from “Around the World in Eighty Days” – discuss how winds mattered.
writing: Write a sailor’s log describing a voyage using only natural wind clues.
more: Build a DIY anemometer from paper cups and straws.
other: Collect weather-station data online; track jet-stream shifts over a week.

title: Clouds & Precipitation (condensation, nucleation, phase changes)
about: Formation of clouds and rain when water vapour condenses around particles.
principles: Condensation nuclei, phase change, latent heat, water cycle.
philosophy: The seen and unseen interweave; tiny seeds of change create visible transformation.
experiments: “Cloud in a Bottle”: warm water + match smoke + squeeze bottle.
home: Watch steam from boiling kettle condense on a cold lid.
outdoors: Cloud-spotting walk; sketch types; record time until rain.
dance: Slow, floating dance as clouds, ending in sudden raindrop leaps.
drama: Mime drama: invisible vapour turning into rain, then snow.
art: Water-colour painting: let pigment bleed like spreading clouds.
music: Percussion rain-storm: start with finger snaps (drizzle) build to drum rolls (downpour).
yoga: Cooling “sheetali” breath; notice moisture in exhale.
physical_games: Drip-drip relay: carry water drops without spilling—imitates raindrop formation.
games: Puzzle: match cloud shapes to weather outcomes.
reading: “The Cloud Book” by Tomie dePaola.
writing: Write a poem from the view of a single raindrop’s journey.
more: Time-lapse photography of an approaching storm front.
other: Build a backyard rain gauge and record daily for a month.

title: Storms (cyclones, hurricanes, tornadoes, monsoons)
about: Intense weather systems where energy from heat and pressure is violently released.
principles: Low-pressure systems, Coriolis rotation, moisture/heat feedback, monsoon dynamics.
philosophy: Power and impermanence; energy can create and destroy; chaos has pattern.
experiments: Bottle tornado: two plastic bottles joined, swirl water.
home: Listen to recordings of real storms; compare with calm indoor sounds.
outdoors: Safely watch a distant thunderstorm; map lightning–thunder gap to gauge distance.
dance: High-energy group dance: swirling arms, sudden stops for thunderclaps.
drama: Drama: villagers preparing for a monsoon, each with different feelings of fear and hope.
art: Charcoal drawing of lightning against dark sky.
music: Create a “storm symphony” with drums, shakers, and sudden silences.
physical_games: “Cyclone chase”: kids run in spirals then burst outward when whistle blows.
games: Cooperative card game: players must “balance” resources to survive an approaching storm.
reading: Read “Eye of the Storm” by Marcia Amidon Lusted (kid’s science book).
writing: Write a first-person diary as the “Eye of the Cyclone.”
more: Build a simple weather alert poster for your neighbourhood.
other: Interview an elder about memories of big storms.

title: Climate Zones & Classification
about: How Earth’s regions differ in temperature, rainfall, vegetation.
principles: Köppen climate types, latitude/altitude effects, ocean currents.
philosophy: Diversity creates balance; many paths to sustain life.
experiments: Compare soil and leaf samples from different garden micro-climates (sunny vs shady).
home: Keep a week-long log of indoor/outdoor temperatures and humidity.
outdoors: Map a park noting warm vs cool, wet vs dry spots.
dance: Group dance: each kid embodies a different climate (desert stillness, rainforest sway).
drama: Drama: council of climates debating how to share the planet.
art: Paint a world map showing different climate belts in chosen colours.
music: Compose short tunes capturing the “feel” of tundra, desert, rainforest.
yoga: Slow, grounding “mountain pose” (tadasana) to sense stability across climates.
physical_games: “Climate tag”: zones of the playground marked as desert/rainforest—rules change with zone.
games: Trivia quiz: match animal/plant cards to the right climate.
reading: “One Well” by Rochelle Strauss (global water & climate).
writing: Write a story about a traveler experiencing all five climate zones in one year.
more: Create a mini terrarium and a dry sand bottle—compare over weeks.
other: Collect weather data from different world cities and graph patterns.

title: Temperature, Humidity, Pressure
about-the-concept: Heat energy, moisture in air and the invisible weight of the atmosphere together drive weather and life.
principles-within-the-concept: Heat transfer and kinetic theory; evaporation/condensation and water-vapour capacity; gas laws and pressure gradients.
philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: Change is constant; unseen forces hold systems in balance; life depends on dynamic equilibrium.
experiments: Build a solar oven from a pizza box and track how inside temperature rises and falls with cloud cover; create a mini-cloud in a jar using warm water, incense smoke and an ice pack; make a barograph by stretching a balloon over a jar and attaching a pen to record pressure changes.
activities-around-the-house: Map micro-climates in your home by measuring temperatures in fridge, sunny sill and bathroom after a shower; tape a plastic bag over a leafy plant overnight to watch moisture collect; mark the Sun’s shadow every 8 minutes to feel the pace of heat change.
activities-outside-the-house-in-nature: Take a dawn walk to feel the temperature drop and observe dew; climb a hill or tall building and record ear-popping plus thermometer change to sense lower pressure; watch a river or lake as mist lifts when the Sun warms the air.
dance: Group choreography moving from “frozen molecules” to “rapid heat swirl”; breath-driven movement—slow cool inhale, fast hot exhale; partner dance showing warm air expanding and cool air sinking.
drama: Short play where Heat, Moisture and Air Pressure debate who creates weather; mime a storm forming from invisible cues; role-play a molecule’s journey from ice to vapour.
painting-drawing: Thermochromic art or two-colour watercolours that change when wet; draw a poster of “invisible forces” with pressure arrows and humidity clouds; make dew-drop prints on dark paper in early morning.
music: Compose a “barometric symphony” with deep drums for high pressure and airy flutes for low; record dripping taps and kettle whistles to create a humidity soundscape; use glasses of water at different fill levels to play a “temperature scale.”
yoga-breathing: Practise sheetali (cooling breath) followed by kapalabhati (heating breath) to feel body temperature shift; alternate-nostril breathing to balance internal pressure; slow pranayama visualising warm air rising.
physical_games: “Pressure Tag”: crouch as low-pressure until rescued by a high-pressure player; water-balloon humidity relay; “hot–cold chase” where caller shouts “heat wave” or “cold front.”
games-of-any-kind: Create a board game where players race storm fronts using temperature and pressure cards; “guess-the-reading” contest with hidden thermometer/hygrometer; Weather Jeopardy with categories for temperature, humidity and pressure.
reading: Weather by Seymour Simon; Clouds, Rain, and Fog by Paul Fleisher; kid-friendly meteorology articles on the water cycle and pressure systems.
writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Diary entry from a drop of water moving through humid air; poem on how the body feels just before rain; short story titled “The Invisible Weight of the Sky.”
more: Build a mini-greenhouse from clear plastic to watch the humidity cycle; take infrared thermometer photos if you have a clip-on sensor; interview grandparents about memorable hot or cold spells and compare with today’s data.
other: Photograph morning condensation on leaves for a week; build a backyard weather station with thermometer, hygrometer and barometer; create a time-lapse of clouds on a warm day.

title: Winds & Circulation (Coriolis effect, trade winds, jet streams)
about-the-concept: Global and local air movements shaped by Earth’s rotation and uneven heating.
principles-within-the-concept: Coriolis effect deflecting moving air; pressure belts and Hadley cells; jet-stream dynamics.
philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: Movement and rotation create large-scale order; invisible motion links continents and climates.
experiments: Spin a Lazy Susan or turntable while drawing a straight chalk line to show Coriolis deflection; make a two-bowl convection cell with a candle and ice to visualise Hadley circulation; track wind direction daily using a homemade anemometer and ribbon wind vane.
activities-around-the-house: Use incense smoke and a table fan to reveal mini air-currents; create a fleet of paper helicopters and observe how draughts in different rooms affect flight; set up a “wind tunnel” using a large cardboard box and small fan to test paper gliders.
activities-outside-the-house-in-nature: Fly kites and log how gusts change with kite altitude; walk on a beach or open field with ribbons to map micro-currents; record local wind data and compare with online jet-stream forecasts over a week.
dance: Spiral dance with arms wide turning like Earth to trace air currents; partner dance imitating opposing trade winds; group movement creating a “jet-stream ribbon” in the air.
drama: Skit: “East Wind meets West Wind” debating who brings the rains; dramatise a sailor using the trade winds to cross an ocean; act out a day in the life of a jet-stream.
painting-drawing: Paint a world map with swirling arrows of global wind belts; create abstract art of spiral storms using only blue and white; make wind-direction calligraphy with ink blown through a straw.
music: Build a wind-chime orchestra and let real gusts compose the melody; record outdoor sounds from gentle breeze to strong gust and layer them into a “wind symphony”; improvise music where tempo follows wind-speed readings.
yoga-breathing: Practise long slow “wind breath”: inhale with arms up, exhale twisting like a cyclone; dynamic breathing paired with slow spins to feel Coriolis rotation; alternate fast/slow breathing to mimic gusts.
physical_games: Parachute game: children create waves of “wind belts” with a large sheet; “trade-wind tag” where players can only move in curved paths; relay race where each lap must be run while spinning to feel deflection.
games-of-any-kind: Design a sailing-race board game where players use trade-wind cards to move; puzzle where pieces must be placed following a Coriolis spiral; trivia game matching wind names to world regions.
reading: Around the World in Eighty Days (discuss reliance on winds); kid-friendly books on global weather patterns; NASA Earth Observatory articles on jet streams.
writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Write a sailor’s log describing a voyage using only natural wind clues; poem comparing a gentle breeze to the power of the jet stream; short story of a leaf’s journey in the upper atmosphere.
more: Build a DIY anemometer from paper cups and straws; collect real weather-station data and plot local wind roses; interview a pilot or sailor about how they read winds.
other: Create a time-lapse video of cloud movement to visualise wind; photograph tree movements at different times of day; map your town’s windy spots on a shared digital map.

title: Seasonal cycles (tilt, precession, Milankovitch cycles)
about-the-concept: Earth’s axial tilt and slow wobble create seasons and long-term climate rhythms.
principles-within-the-concept: 23.5° tilt causes seasons; precession and orbital eccentricity alter climate over thousands of years.
philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: Cycles of change and return; time is not linear but rhythmic; subtle motions create profound effects.
experiments: Tilt a globe and shine a lamp to model seasons; mark midday shadow length through a year; freeze a wet string on a spinning ball to show precession visually.
activities-around-the-house: Keep a year-long journal of sunrise/sunset times and indoor light changes; create a season calendar with household temperature/humidity records; use ice-cube trays to track how freezer frost varies over months.
activities-outside-the-house-in-nature: Visit a park at solstice and equinox to record sun angle; photograph the same tree each month to show seasonal change; build a stone “mini henge” and watch shadows shift.
dance: Four-part dance moving from spring’s budding to winter’s stillness; spiral movement representing Earth’s slow wobble; rhythmic circle dance marking solstices.
drama: Skit of Sun and Earth negotiating the length of seasons; play about a community preparing for solstice rituals; mime the long slow wobble of precession.
painting-drawing: Draw the Sun’s path across the sky for each season; paint a year-wheel mandala; make a colour chart of monthly sunrise hues.
music: Compose a piece that speeds and slows to mimic orbital cycles; create a soundscape of birdsongs from different seasons; use percussion to mark the solstice rhythm.
yoga-breathing: Practice Surya Namaskar at sunrise in each season to feel the light difference; slow breathing while visualising the Earth’s annual journey; alternate fast/slow breaths to represent changing seasons.
physical_games: “Season switch” relay: players must change costume pieces to match shouted season; shadow-length limbo; running race with timed “equinox” pauses.
games-of-any-kind: Board game where players advance only when their planet card reaches the correct orbital position; trivia game matching world festivals to solstices/equinoxes; jigsaw of Milankovitch cycles timeline.
reading: The Long Thaw by David Archer (simplified extracts); children’s books on solstices and equinoxes; NASA climate cycle resources.
writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Journal your own seasonal mood shifts; poem from the perspective of Earth’s tilted axis; story of a future astronomer explaining precession to kids.
more: Build a permanent sundial and record noon shadow throughout the year; photograph identical landscape shots monthly to capture seasonal light; track constellation positions seasonally.
other: Create time-lapse of garden from equinox to solstice; interview farmers or gardeners about seasonal cues; visit a planetarium for a precession show.

title: Energy balance of Earth (incoming solar, outgoing IR)
about-the-concept: The planet stays habitable by balancing sunlight absorbed and infrared energy released.
principles-within-the-concept: Albedo and reflectivity; greenhouse effect; radiation balance and feedbacks.
philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: Harmony requires give and take; too much imbalance brings instability; invisible flows maintain life.
experiments: Compare temperatures of dark vs white cloth in sunlight; build a simple radiometer or use an infrared thermometer to measure ground cooling after sunset; create a mini greenhouse from clear plastic to track heat trapping.
activities-around-the-house: Place thermometers in sunny and shaded windows to log heat gain; wrap jars in black/white paper to see which warms faster; use kitchen foil vs. dark plate to show heat radiation differences.
activities-outside-the-house-in-nature: Night-time field trip: measure surface cooling rates in different terrains; compare temperature of asphalt vs. grass; observe urban heat-island effect in city park.
dance: Dance contrasting bright reflective movements with slow heat-release motions; group choreography of “energy in/energy out.”
drama: Play where Sun and Earth argue over balance of energy; dramatic debate of clouds vs. ice about who reflects most light; enact a greenhouse negotiation.
painting-drawing: Paint an “energy map” of Earth with arrows for solar input and IR output; create two half-canvas paintings—one bright, one dark—to show albedo.
music: Compose music alternating high-pitched “sunlight” notes and low “infrared” tones; create a call-and-response piece symbolising energy exchange; record day-night outdoor sounds for a balance duet.
yoga-breathing: Practice alternate-nostril breathing imagining sunlight in, infrared out; breath-retention to feel internal heat balance; slow cooling pranayama at night.
physical_games: “Albedo tag”: children in white shirts reflect (immune from tag) while dark shirts absorb (taggers’ target); relay race moving energy tokens from Sun to Earth and back; hot-cold scavenger hunt.
games-of-any-kind: Build a cooperative board game where players must keep Earth’s energy budget stable; card game matching surfaces to their albedo; quiz on heat-island hotspots.
reading: Energy Balance of Earth (NASA resources); kids’ guides to greenhouse effect; simple texts on urban heat islands.
writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Diary entry from a photon entering Earth’s atmosphere; poem about the dance of sunlight and darkness; story of a planet that lost its balance.
more: Construct a DIY pyranometer to measure sunlight intensity; use satellite imagery (public datasets) to compare snow vs. ocean albedo; photograph city heat at night with a thermal camera if available.
other: Host a “balance the planet” role-play council where kids represent Sun, clouds, oceans, ice; visit a science museum climate exhibit; collect infrared satellite images online.

title: Ocean–atmosphere interactions (El Niño, La Niña, monsoon)
about-the-concept: Exchanges of heat and moisture between ocean and air drive events like monsoons and El Niño.
principles-within-the-concept: ENSO cycles; ocean heat transport; pressure and wind feedbacks.
philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: Ocean and sky are a single breathing system; distant events are linked; local weather is global.
experiments: Set up a shallow pan with warm and cold water to show convection currents; demonstrate monsoon rain using a kettle for evaporation and a chilled plate for condensation; build a “mini-El Niño” with a heated fish tank and ice pack to watch current reversal.
activities-around-the-house: Track daily sea-surface temperatures online and compare to local rainfall; create a wall map with strings linking your town’s weather to Pacific Ocean data; keep a rain diary during monsoon.
activities-outside-the-house-in-nature: Visit a coastal area to feel sea breezes; stand on a pier during changing tides; observe humidity before and after a thunderstorm.
dance: Flowing group dance where half the dancers move as ocean currents and half as atmospheric winds; duet of warm vs. cold currents.
drama: Skit of a conversation between Ocean and Atmosphere deciding global weather; role-play villagers awaiting monsoon rains; act out El Niño warming vs. La Niña cooling.
painting-drawing: Paint the Pacific with warm/cold patches to show El Niño pattern; draw a monsoon cloudburst with swirling arrows; create a poster linking faraway oceans to local rains.
music: Create a drum circle that alternates between calm ocean beats and sudden storm crescendos; compose a piece where rhythm follows ENSO cycle phases; use rainsticks to mimic monsoon onset.
yoga-breathing: Practice ocean-breathing pranayama with slow wave-like inhalations; “sea breeze breath”—inhale imagining cool ocean air, exhale warm land air; gentle yoga flow timed to wave sounds.
physical_games: “Monsoon relay”: carry water cups while dodging “wind gust” players; “current chase” where players move only in curved paths; tug-of-war representing shifting trade winds.
games-of-any-kind: Design a strategy game where players manage crops during unpredictable El Niño years; matching cards of world regions to ENSO impacts; jigsaw of monsoon circulation map.
reading: El Niño and La Niña Explained (NOAA kid resources); books on Indian monsoon stories; simple oceanography texts.
writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Journal about how distant oceans might change your hometown weather; poem from the viewpoint of a warm Pacific current; letter from a farmer awaiting monsoon rains.
more: Create a backyard rain gauge and compare with global ENSO forecasts; build a simple tide pool model; track real-time satellite images of sea-surface temperature.
other: Interview a fisherman or farmer about monsoon experiences; watch live coastal webcams during storm surges; visit an aquarium with an ocean current exhibit.

title: Climate feedbacks (ice-albedo, greenhouse effect, carbon cycle)
about-the-concept: Loops where climate change accelerates or slows itself.
principles-within-the-concept: Ice-albedo positive feedback; greenhouse gas concentration; carbon sinks and sources.
philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: Actions have consequences; small changes can amplify; interconnectedness of all living systems.
experiments: Compare melt rate of ice on black cloth vs white cloth to show albedo; bottle two mini-greenhouses—one sealed with CO₂ from vinegar & baking soda, one normal—and measure temperature difference; use yeast in a bottle with balloon to visualise carbon cycle gas release.
activities-around-the-house: Keep a daily CO₂ log from a cheap indoor sensor; compost kitchen scraps and measure temperature rise; monitor houseplant growth as a carbon sink.
activities-outside-the-house-in-nature: Walk in a forest and measure cooler temps vs nearby asphalt; observe snow or frost reflecting sunlight; collect autumn leaves and track their decay.
dance: Dance showing the feedback loop: ice retreat leads to more heat, leading to faster retreat; group movement of “carbon molecules” cycling through earth, air, plants.
drama: Drama of a council of Earth systems debating how to keep balance; skit of greenhouse gases discussing their power; role-play carbon atoms moving through atmosphere and biosphere.
painting-drawing: Paint a before/after polar landscape showing loss of ice; create a carbon-cycle infographic mural; draw a greenhouse with layers of trapping gases.
music: Compose music that starts with soft reflective tones and builds to a heat crescendo; create a carbon-cycle rap; percussion piece rising in tempo to mimic accelerating feedback.
yoga-breathing: Practice cooling breath and warming breath in sequence to feel feedback; tree-pose meditation reflecting stability vs change; pranayama while visualising carbon moving through you.
physical_games: “Feedback chase”: tag game where each tagger adds another player to show positive feedback; “carbon cycle relay”: players carry “carbon tokens” through plant–animal–air stations; hot–cold freeze dance representing warming and cooling phases.
games-of-any-kind: Cooperative board game where players must keep global temperature stable; card game matching feedback type to effect; trivia quiz on carbon sinks and sources.
reading: Our Changing Climate by National Geographic Kids; articles on ice-albedo feedback and carbon cycle; NASA Earth Observatory pieces.
writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Diary entry from an ice sheet watching itself shrink; poem about a carbon atom’s long journey; essay: “How my choices feed back into Earth’s climate.”
more: Build a terrarium to observe plant carbon uptake; use satellite images to track polar ice over months; create a school exhibit showing positive and negative feedbacks.
other: Interview an environmental scientist; watch a documentary on Arctic ice loss; visit a botanical garden to discuss carbon storage.

title: Ice ages & paleoclimate
about-the-concept: Evidence from past climates shows Earth’s long swings between warm and frozen eras.
principles-within-the-concept: Ice-core analysis, sediment records, isotope ratios; orbital forcing (Milankovitch cycles).
philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: The past is a teacher; Earth’s memory is stored in layers; long timescales humble human perspective.
experiments: Freeze layers of coloured water to model ice cores and drill with a straw; make a sand-and-shell jar to show sediment layering; use a simple microscope to examine air bubbles in old ice chips.
activities-around-the-house: Create a “timeline wall” marking major ice ages with household items as markers; compare freezer frost layers week by week; keep a “mini-ice age” diary of your fridge temperature.
activities-outside-the-house-in-nature: Hike to a glacial moraine or riverbed to see old ice-age rocks; visit a local cave to view stalactites as climate archives; observe fossil beds if available.
dance: Slow-motion dance representing ice advancing and retreating; partner dance where one melts while the other freezes; circular movement showing repeated glacial cycles.
drama: Skit of scientists extracting an ice core and hearing voices of ancient air; drama of Earth recounting its own climate history; role-play of a carbon atom trapped in ice for millennia.
painting-drawing: Paint a layered mural of ice-core bands; draw a world map showing maximum ice-sheet extents; create an abstract “deep time” timeline art.
music: Compose a “deep time” piece with long slow tones and sudden warming crescendos; use percussion to mark each glacial advance; create a sound collage from natural icy recordings.
yoga-breathing: Practice long slow breathing imagining thousand-year cycles; mountain pose to embody geologic time; meditation on patience and change.
physical_games: “Glacier tag”: players slowly expand to capture space like advancing ice; freeze–thaw game with sudden warm periods; relay representing sediment deposition.
games-of-any-kind: Quiz game matching geological periods to key climate events; board game where players must survive shifting ice ages; jigsaw of a paleoclimate graph.
reading: Ice Ages: Past and Future by Richard Alley (simplified excerpts); kid-friendly articles on ice cores and fossils; National Geographic features on paleoclimate.
writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Poem from the view of an ancient ice crystal; story of a mammoth describing its frozen world; essay on what humans can learn from deep-time climate records.
more: Build a simple “ice core” display for school; examine real fossil samples or visit a museum; time-lapse your own freezer frost as a mini paleoclimate record.
other: Interview a local geologist; watch a documentary on glaciation; explore a science centre with paleoclimate exhibits.

title: Greenhouse gases & global warming
about-the-concept: Certain gases trap heat, causing Earth’s temperature to rise.
principles-within-the-concept: Greenhouse effect; anthropogenic CO₂ and methane sources; energy imbalance.
philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: Actions ripple globally; stewardship is shared responsibility; small changes matter.
experiments: Two-bottle greenhouse experiment: one bottle filled with CO₂ from vinegar & baking soda warms faster under a lamp; compare clear vs. covered jar temperature rise; build a simple infrared thermometer circuit to track heat.
activities-around-the-house: Audit your household for CO₂ sources—lights, appliances—and chart reductions; grow indoor plants to act as carbon sinks; measure temperature differences between shaded and sunlit windows.
activities-outside-the-house-in-nature: Take a walk in a city park and compare temperatures of asphalt vs. grass; visit a landfill to observe methane capture if tours are offered; monitor local air-quality index.
dance: Dance moving from cool blue to fiery red to show rising global temperatures; group improvisation where dancers act as greenhouse gases thickening around the Earth.
drama: Drama of a council of greenhouse gases debating their effects; role-play a UN climate summit; skit of future children sending messages back to today.
painting-drawing: Paint a “before and after” Earth showing pre-industrial and modern atmosphere; create a poster of major greenhouse gases and their sources; draw a heat map of your city.
music: Compose a rap about greenhouse gases; soundscape mixing industrial noises with bird songs fading; create a music piece whose volume rises to mimic global warming.
yoga-breathing: Practice “fire breath” (kapalabhati) to feel internal heat; cooling breath to counter it; yoga flow reflecting balance between warming and cooling.
physical_games: “Carbon capture” tag: runners collect “carbon tokens” before taggers; relay race where each lap represents a decade of warming; hot-potato game symbolising rising temperatures.
games-of-any-kind: Cooperative board game where players reduce emissions to keep global temperature below 2 °C; trivia quiz on greenhouse gases; card game matching sources to gases.
reading: Our House Is on Fire (Greta Thunberg’s family story adapted for kids); kid-friendly guides to greenhouse effect and climate change; NASA Climate Kids website.
writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Letter to future grandchildren about what you did for the planet; poem on a single CO₂ molecule’s journey; essay “How my choices change Earth’s temperature.”
more: Plant a tree and record its growth as a living carbon sink; set up a school-wide “no-plastic week”; track local temperature records over decades from public data.
other: Join a community clean-up; visit a renewable-energy site; watch a documentary such as Before the Flood and discuss actions.

title: Human impact (anthropogenic forcing, aerosols)
about-the-concept: Human activities—burning fuel, industry, land use—alter climate by adding greenhouse gases and particles.
principles-within-the-concept: Radiative forcing; aerosol scattering; feedback loops between human behaviour and climate.
philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: Our choices ripple through Earth systems; responsibility and interconnection.
experiments: Build two identical mini-greenhouses—one with added smoke or aerosol from a safe incense stick—to compare temperature; test visibility by shining a laser through clear vs. smoky jar; measure indoor CO₂ with a cheap sensor before and after people gather.
activities-around-the-house: Conduct a “household emissions audit” (electricity use, travel, cooking); create a weekly low-carbon menu; make a DIY air filter and check collected particles.
activities-outside-the-house-in-nature: Visit a busy street and a park to compare air quality using simple particulate counters; photograph haze at sunrise and midday; join a tree-planting drive.
dance: Group dance shifting from chaotic industrial motions to slow regenerative ones; duet where one dancer scatters like aerosols while another clears the air.
drama: Skit of “Earth on trial” where children play lawyers for and against human actions; role-play of future citizens pleading with present humans.
painting-drawing: Draw a before/after cityscape—clear sky vs. smog; create infographics of global emissions; paint the invisible “cloud” of human influence.
music: Compose a piece starting with factory clatter and resolving into natural sounds; create a percussion rhythm using recycled metal to symbolise industry.
yoga-breathing: Alternate slow cooling breaths and fast heating breaths to embody climate swings; “breath audit”: notice indoor air quality while breathing mindfully.
physical_games: “Pollution tag”: players with grey scarves represent aerosols that spread by tagging others; relay race carrying “carbon tokens” to illustrate emissions.
games-of-any-kind: Cooperative board game where players must cut emissions before time runs out; trivia quiz on climate impacts; matching cards of human activities to their forcing effects.
reading: This Changes Everything (adapted summaries for kids/teens); NASA Climate Kids articles on aerosols; IPCC children’s guides.
writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Diary of an air molecule passing through factories and forests; poem about human fingerprints on the sky; essay on personal responsibility for climate.

other: Interview elders about how local air and seasons have changed; visit a renewable-energy site; watch a short documentary on aerosols.

title: Climate models & predictions
about-the-concept: Scientists use computer models to simulate Earth’s climate and forecast future changes.

philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: The future is not fixed; knowledge allows foresight and stewardship.

activities-around-the-house: Keep a notebook of daily weather, then compare with professional forecasts; use spreadsheet to graph temperature trends at home; simulate greenhouse effect with two jars and lamps.
activities-outside-the-house-in-nature: Visit a weather station or university meteorology lab; attend a public lecture on climate science; observe how local forecasts match reality over weeks.
dance: Dance where each movement represents a climate variable—temperature, sea level, ice cover—changing with music tempo; group improvisation showing positive and negative feedbacks.
drama: Drama of a team of future scientists explaining model predictions to world leaders; courtroom play debating different emissions scenarios.
painting-drawing: Paint “possible futures”: contrasting canvases for high vs. low emissions paths; create a climate data mural with graphs and icons.
music: Compose music where instruments enter one by one like variables in a model; use electronic loops to build complexity over time.
yoga-breathing: Practice visualisation meditation: imagine Earth under different future scenarios; breath work to embody rising and falling climate patterns.
physical_games: “Scenario tag”: each team represents a scenario (high/low emissions) and must reach a goal before “time” runs out; data-hunt relay using real climate datasets.
games-of-any-kind: Board game where players adjust variables (CO₂, forests, oceans) and see resulting temperature changes; puzzle assembling a climate feedback diagram; trivia game on famous climate predictions.
reading: How to Change Everything by Naomi Klein (youth edition); NOAA resources on climate modelling; NASA Earth Science outreach material.
writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Write a letter from a future child describing life under a chosen climate scenario; poem about “tomorrow’s weather” fifty years from now; short story where a climate model speaks as a character.
more: Code a simple spreadsheet climate model; analyse open climate datasets; create a school exhibit comparing forecasts to observed trends.
other: Interview a meteorologist; watch a documentary on supercomputers in climate science; visit a planetarium climate show.

title: Atoms, Molecules
about-the-concept: Basic building blocks of matter: atoms combine to form molecules.
principles-within-the-concept: Atomic theory; chemical bonding; conservation of matter.
philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: Unity beneath diversity; everything visible is built from the same few ingredients.
experiments: Grow salt or sugar crystals to watch molecules arrange; split water into hydrogen and oxygen with a simple electrolysis kit; build 3-D models of common molecules with clay or candy.
activities-around-the-house: Use kitchen ingredients to model molecules with coloured beads or pasta; freeze and melt water observing molecules’ behaviour; compare scents of different spices as molecular signals.
activities-outside-the-house-in-nature: Nature walk: collect leaves or rocks and discuss molecular makeup; visit a science museum with atomic exhibits; observe dew to discuss water molecules.
dance: Group dance where each child is an atom bonding to form molecules; “gas to liquid” movement sequence showing molecular spacing.
drama: Skit of atoms at a party forming different molecule “friendships”; drama of hydrogen and oxygen meeting to create water.
painting-drawing: Draw molecular structures as geometric art; paint abstract patterns inspired by molecular lattices; create “periodic table collage.”
music: Compose music with repeating motifs to represent molecular patterns; create a soundscape where different instruments are different atoms.
yoga-breathing: Slow, mindful breathing while visualising molecules moving in and out of lungs; “molecular breath” meditation imagining air particles entering the body.
physical_games: “Molecule tag”: atoms (players) must find partners to form specified molecules; relay race forming H₂O or CO₂ groups.
games-of-any-kind: Card-matching game of molecule formulas to names; board game assembling molecules for points; 3-D puzzle building crystal structures.
reading: Stuff Matters by Mark Miodownik (selected passages for kids); simple chemistry picture books; Royal Society of Chemistry outreach materials.
writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Poem from an oxygen atom’s point of view; short story where molecules tell their life cycle; observation journal of everyday materials and their molecular makeup.
more: Visit a local chemistry lab; make homemade playdough molecules; photograph snowflakes to discuss molecular symmetry.
other: Attend a public chemistry show; watch atomic-scale animations online; interview a chemist about molecular design.

title: Electrons
about-the-concept: Negatively charged subatomic particles that orbit atomic nuclei and enable chemistry and electricity.
principles-within-the-concept: Quantum behaviour; charge and electromagnetic interactions; energy levels.
philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: Invisible agents connect light and matter; motion of electrons powers life and technology.
experiments: Build a simple lemon battery and light an LED; show electron flow with a hand-cranked generator; observe sparks from a static electricity balloon experiment.
activities-around-the-house: Explore household circuits by safely checking which appliances complete a circuit; test conductivity of different kitchen materials with a battery and bulb; watch LEDs glow brighter/dimmer with different resistors.
activities-outside-the-house-in-nature: Visit a power station or science centre electricity exhibit; observe lightning during a storm; use a handheld Van de Graaff generator if available.
dance: Dance representing electrons jumping between energy levels—small leaps for low energy, big leaps for high; spiral movement imitating electron clouds.
drama: Skit of electrons carrying messages between atoms; drama of an electron’s journey through a wire to light a bulb.
painting-drawing: Draw electron clouds using swirling dots; paint energy-level diagrams in abstract art; create neon-coloured electron tracks on black paper.
music: Compose electronic music with sudden jumps in pitch for electron transitions; create a beat using crackling static sounds; improvise a “current flow” rhythm.
yoga-breathing: Practice rapid “kapalabhati” breath to mimic electron energy bursts; alternate fast and slow breaths representing electron transitions; visualise electrons moving with each inhale/exhale.
physical_games: “Current chase”: players form a human circuit and pass a squeeze to represent electron flow; static balloon hair-raising contest; relay race carrying “charge tokens.”
games-of-any-kind: Build a simple circuit-board game where correct connections light LEDs; trivia quiz on electron discoveries; card game matching subatomic particles to properties.
reading: Electric Universe by David Bodanis (selected kid-friendly sections); introductory books on electricity and magnetism; kid-level quantum physics resources.
writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Diary of an electron travelling through a circuit; poem about a lightning bolt’s electrons; story of an electron jumping energy levels.
more: Construct a homemade electromagnet; photograph lightning or spark discharges; watch electron microscope images online.
other: Interview an electrician about current flow; attend a science centre show on electricity; build a DIY radio kit.

title: Atomic Structure
about-the-concept: Atoms have a dense nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons in energy shells.
principles-within-the-concept: Nuclear forces; quantum orbitals; periodic table organisation.
philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: Hidden order within chaos; strength and stability arise from balanced forces.
experiments: Build Bohr model with beads and wire; scatter small magnets to model electron shells; use cloud chamber or online video to visualise particle tracks.
activities-around-the-house: Create a 3-D atom model from household materials; colour-code kitchen items by elements they contain; arrange pantry items into “periodic table” groups.
activities-outside-the-house-in-nature: Visit a nuclear science museum; look at minerals through a hand lens to discuss atomic makeup; attend a planetarium show on subatomic particles.
dance: Choreograph a dance of electrons jumping shells; group circle dance representing nucleus stability; slow orbital movements for electron paths.
drama: Drama of protons and neutrons debating who holds the nucleus together; role-play of electrons negotiating energy levels; skit of the periodic table coming alive.
painting-drawing: Draw atom cross-sections with concentric energy levels; paint abstract electron orbitals; create a mosaic of periodic table symbols.
music: Create a percussion piece where each beat represents an electron orbital; electronic music with sudden key changes for shell transitions; compose a nucleus–electron call-and-response.
yoga-breathing: Practice “atomic breath”: visualise breath as electrons moving in shells; slow pranayama focusing on centre (nucleus) and periphery (electrons).
physical_games: “Shell tag”: players move in concentric circles around a “nucleus” person; relay game where electrons must jump to higher shells when called.
games-of-any-kind: Board game building atoms from protons, neutrons and electrons; puzzle matching element symbols to atomic numbers; trivia quiz on atomic discoveries.
reading: The Elements by Theodore Gray; kid-friendly atomic physics books; Royal Institution videos on atoms.
writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Poem describing the hidden architecture of an atom; story of a neutron inside the nucleus; journal entry imagining the life of a proton.
more: Build a simple Geiger counter kit; photograph crystals and link to atomic lattices; watch cloud chamber demonstrations online.
other: Interview a physicist about atomic research; visit a particle accelerator exhibit; build an interactive periodic table wall.

title: Atomic collisions
about-the-concept: When atoms or subatomic particles collide, they exchange energy and can form new particles or radiation.
principles-within-the-concept: Conservation of momentum and energy; nuclear reactions; particle interactions.
philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: Interactions create change; even the tiniest encounters can transform reality.
experiments: Use two marbles on a track to demonstrate elastic collisions; observe sparks in a static electricity discharge; watch online cloud chamber videos of particle tracks.
activities-around-the-house: Play marble collision games and measure rebound distances; use a pendulum (Newton’s cradle) to show momentum transfer; test how different materials affect bounce.
activities-outside-the-house-in-nature: Watch meteor showers to imagine atomic-scale collisions; visit a science centre particle accelerator demo; observe cosmic rays in a cloud chamber exhibit.
dance: Fast-paced group dance of sudden impacts and rebounds; duet representing two particles colliding and merging.
drama: Drama of two atoms meeting and creating a new element; skit of protons smashing in a collider; mime the Big Bang particle dance.
painting-drawing: Paint abstract “collision” art with splatter techniques; draw cloud chamber tracks; create a comic strip of particle adventures.
music: Create a percussion piece of sudden sharp beats representing collisions; improvise music with abrupt dynamic changes; record clashing metallic sounds for a sound collage.
yoga-breathing: Practice breath bursts (short sharp exhales) to mimic collision impacts; dynamic yoga flows with sudden stops; visualise energy release in meditation.
physical_games: “Particle tag”: players collide gently and exchange roles; marble run race where collisions score points; human Newton’s cradle.
games-of-any-kind: Design a board game where particle collisions create new “elements”; puzzle matching collision types to outcomes; trivia quiz on famous physics experiments.
reading: Smash! Exploring the Mysteries of the Universe by Sara Latta; CERN kids’ resources on particle physics; simple books on nuclear science.
writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Poem from the perspective of two colliding particles; story about the first moments of the universe; observation journal after watching cloud chamber footage.
more: Build a small cloud chamber at home with dry ice; photograph meteor shower streaks; make slow-motion videos of balloon pops as macro-collisions.
other: Interview a physicist about particle colliders; attend a science festival with accelerator demos; watch a documentary on the Large Hadron Collider.

title: Molecular Structure
about-the-concept: How atoms arrange and bond to form molecules with specific shapes and properties.
principles-within-the-concept: Covalent and ionic bonding; molecular geometry; polarity and intermolecular forces.
philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: Form follows function; patterns in structure determine behaviour; beauty of hidden geometry.
experiments: Grow sugar crystals to show ordered molecular lattices; make 3-D molecular models from marshmallows and toothpicks; examine soap bubbles to discuss molecular surface tension.
activities-around-the-house: Build paper or clay models of complex molecules; test solubility of different household substances; compare scents of essential oils as examples of molecular shape affecting smell.
activities-outside-the-house-in-nature: Walk in a botanical garden and discuss plant aromas and molecular causes; collect minerals and examine crystal faces; observe snowflakes under a magnifier to see molecular symmetry.
dance: Dance where each group of dancers forms different geometric shapes (tetrahedral, linear, bent) representing molecules; partner improvisation to show polarity attraction.
drama: Skit of molecules forming different compounds and reacting; drama of water molecules bonding and breaking in a storm; role-play of DNA strands pairing.
painting-drawing: Paint molecular geometries as abstract art; draw snowflake patterns; create a collage of different molecular structures.
music: Compose music with repeating motifs to represent symmetrical molecules; improvise a melody where instruments “bond” in duets; create a rhythm game where beats represent molecular vibrations.
yoga-breathing: Practice slow breathing while visualising molecular bonds forming and breaking; yoga flow where poses represent molecular shapes; meditation on hidden order.
physical_games: “Molecule freeze dance”: children must form specific geometric shapes when music stops; relay forming H₂O or CO₂ groups; human model of a crystal lattice.
games-of-any-kind: Board game where players collect atoms to build target molecules; card game matching molecular shapes to properties; jigsaw of complex molecular structures.
reading: Molecules: The Elements and the Architecture of Everything by Theodore Gray; simple chemistry picture books; Royal Society of Chemistry outreach.
writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Poem from the view of a single water molecule; story about the making of a perfume molecule; journal describing patterns found in nature and molecules.
more: Visit a chemistry lab or science centre with molecular models; make a 3-D printed molecule if equipment is available; photograph frost patterns as molecular art.
other: Interview a chemist about molecular design; attend a public lecture on nanotechnology; watch molecular dynamics animations online.

title: Other Elementary Particles
about-the-concept: Beyond protons, neutrons and electrons lie neutrinos, quarks, muons and more—the building blocks of matter and forces.
principles-within-the-concept: Standard Model of particle physics; fundamental forces; particle interactions.
philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: Reality hides layers within layers; even the tiniest pieces are dynamic and relational.
experiments: Watch online cloud-chamber videos of muon tracks; build a simple cloud chamber with dry ice to see cosmic rays; use two magnets to model quark colour charges.
activities-around-the-house: Create “particle cards” with properties like charge and spin; build quark models from coloured beads; watch a documentary clip and summarise each particle’s role.
activities-outside-the-house-in-nature: Observe a meteor shower and discuss cosmic-ray particles; visit a science museum with particle accelerator exhibit; attend a public physics lecture.
dance: Group dance showing quarks combining into protons; improvisation of particle collisions; slow movement of elusive neutrinos.
drama: Skit of the Standard Model particles introducing themselves; courtroom drama of forces debating which is strongest; role-play of a neutrino passing through Earth.

music: Compose an electronic piece with sudden “quantum jumps”; layer random percussive sounds to mimic particle interactions; create a soundscape of high-energy collisions.
yoga-breathing: Quick “burst breathing” to mimic particle interactions; dynamic yoga flows with sudden pauses; visualise neutrinos streaming through your body.
physical_games: “Particle tag”: players representing particles collide and exchange roles; human Feynman diagram game; relay representing quarks forming hadrons.
games-of-any-kind: Trivia quiz on elementary particles; board game collecting quarks to build protons; card-matching forces to particles.
reading: Smash! Exploring the Mysteries of the Universe by Sara Latta; CERN’s kids’ particle resources; popular-science books on the Standard Model.
writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Poem from the view of a travelling neutrino; story about quarks arguing over colour charge; diary entry of a muon racing through space.
more: Build a mini particle-accelerator model from magnets; create a particle-family tree poster; visit a planetarium particle show.
other: Interview a physicist; watch a live-stream from CERN; explore interactive particle-physics websites.

title: Crystalline Structures
about-the-concept: Atoms arranged in repeating patterns form crystals—from salt to diamonds.
principles-within-the-concept: Lattice geometry; unit cells; symmetry and defects.
philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: Order emerges from chaos; beauty arises from hidden repetition.
experiments: Grow salt or sugar crystals on a string; examine snowflakes with a magnifier; shine light through crystals to see refraction patterns.
activities-around-the-house: Use kitchen sugar to make rock candy; build paper models of cubic and hexagonal unit cells; photograph crystal patterns in bathroom tiles or window frost.
activities-outside-the-house-in-nature: Collect mineral samples on a hike; visit a gemstone exhibit; observe ice crystals on a cold morning.

music: Compose music with repeating motifs and symmetrical rhythms; create a bell-like chime piece to mimic crystal clarity; improvise canon rounds to show repetition.
yoga-breathing: Practice still, steady breathing while visualising a growing crystal; hold “diamond pose” to feel inner stability; meditation on symmetry.
physical_games: “Lattice tag”: players must hold hands to form repeating shapes; hopscotch arranged in hexagonal pattern; relay forming crystal layers.
games-of-any-kind: Board game where players collect “atoms” to complete crystal cards; puzzle assembling unit-cell shapes; trivia quiz on famous crystals.

writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Poem on the silent growth of a crystal; story of a snowflake’s journey; observation notes of crystal shapes found in nature.
more: Build a kaleidoscope; photograph real crystals under a microscope; create 3-D printed models of lattices.
other: Interview a jeweller or geologist; visit a crystal cave or science museum; watch time-lapse of crystal growth online.

title: X-rays
about-the-concept: High-energy electromagnetic waves that pass through most matter and reveal internal structures.

philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: Hidden truths can be revealed; light beyond the visible carries information.

activities-around-the-house: Examine household items under bright light to guess which parts would show in X-ray; create “shadowgrams” with strong lamp and paper; explore UV vs visible light with cheap UV torch.
activities-outside-the-house-in-nature: Visit a medical imaging centre or science museum X-ray exhibit; observe sunlight scattering through clouds to discuss invisible wavelengths.

music: Compose a piece alternating loud/soft to mirror penetrating vs. absorbed rays; use metallic percussion for “inside view” effect; record and layer echoing sounds.

writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Poem from the perspective of an X-ray; story of bones speaking when seen by invisible light; journal of a scientist discovering X-rays.

other: Interview a radiologist; watch a documentary on X-ray astronomy; visit a hospital imaging department.

title: Lasers & masers
about-the-concept: Devices that produce coherent, focused light or microwaves.

philosophy-underlying-the-concepts: Focused energy shows how order amplifies power; precision through unity.

music: Compose electronic music with perfectly synchronised beats; create a rhythm that begins chaotic then locks into unison; use tuned glasses for harmonic laser-like tones.

physical_games: “Laser tag”: players must move in straight lines; precision relay requiring exact movements; maze run where only straight paths allowed.
games-of-any-kind: Puzzle matching everyday uses of lasers to their technology; trivia quiz on laser inventions; board game where players build a laser path with mirrors.

writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Poem about a single beam of light cutting darkness; story of a photon becoming part of a laser; reflection on the power of focus.

other: Interview a laser engineer; watch a laser light concert; explore online maser astronomy data.

title: Wave basics

writing-observations-stories-poems-answe: Poem about an endless ocean wave; story of a sound travelling across the world; journal of a ripple in a pond.
more: Build a homemade ripple tank; photograph water waves in slow motion; record and analyse sound waveforms on a tablet app.
other: Visit a beach to watch tide waves; attend a concert and discuss sound as waves; explore online simulations of wave interference.
